title: The Megiddo mosaic (the 'God Jesus Christ' inscription)
html:
The Megiddo mosaic (the 'God Jesus Christ' inscription)

c. 230 CE. Source record: Israel Antiquities Authority; Museum of the Bible, Washington.

In 2005, while a new wing was being built at Megiddo prison, excavation exposed a mosaic floor in a building identified as an early Christian prayer hall. The floor carries a Greek inscription that includes the words Θεῷ Ἰησοῦ Χριστῷ — "to God Jesus Christ" — beside a dedication by a Roman officer named Gaianus and the names of women who funded the work.

The mosaic is dated by its pottery, coins, and style to about 230 CE, before Constantine. The floor was lifted and conserved, and was shown at the Museum of the Bible in Washington in 2024-2025 under an agreement with the Israel Antiquities Authority.

What it establishes: a Christian meeting place with an explicitly christological inscription in the third century, and a community in the Jezreel valley of sufficient means to commission mosaic work.

What it does not establish: continuity with Jesus's own ministry, although Megiddo lies in Galilee. The inscription addresses Christ as God, which is a datum for the history of christology, not for the historical Jesus.

The site also yielded a chi-rho and fish motifs in later phases of the same building.
